entries.narration:
Our engine starts as an empty folder called miniflow, and two tools turn it into a project.

The first is Node. In the terminal we ask for its version, and it answers twenty-six point thirteen. The side pane shows what that one command carries. Inside Node is V8, the engine that runs JavaScript, the same one that runs it in Chrome. Around V8 is Node's standard library: files, paths, networking, everything a browser never lets a page touch. When our engine writes a picture to disk, that is the standard library at work.

The second tool is npm, and it ships with Node: the terminal shows its version, eleven point twenty. Its job is the package. We run npm init with the yes flag, which accepts every default, and one more setting that asks for modules. npm would print the whole file it wrote. We send that echo nowhere, because the editor shows the same package dot json. Most of it is a name, a version and an empty test script. The highlighted line is the one that matters to us: type is module. It means every file here uses import and export, the standard JavaScript module syntax, rather than Node's older require.

Down the side pane, npm points the other way, at the registry. That is where the packages we install will come from, starting with TypeScript itself a few sections from now. For the moment, the folder has a package file and nothing else.

Next, we give it a file that draws something.

The first file is main dot ts, and on the right of the explorer it is marked new, along with the picture it writes.

The editor shows its heart. A type called Box describes a box with a title, a width and a height. The box itself is a checkout box, eighty wide and twenty tall, and a padding of twelve goes around it. The three highlighted lines carry types: the shape of a box, the box that must match it, and a padding that must be a number. Below them, the file builds a little SVG string, one rectangle and one line of text, and writes it to a folder called out.

We run it with plain node. No compiler, no build step. Node twenty-six reads a dot ts file directly. The side pane shows how. Node does not check the types at all. It strips them, replacing every annotation with blank space so the line numbers stay put, and hands V8 the JavaScript that is left. V8 runs it, and Node's file system module writes the picture.

The bottom panel is that picture, out slash box dot svg, opened in a browser. One rounded box, one word: checkout. It is a hundred and four by forty-four, the eighty of content plus twelve on each side.

That is the whole engine for now: a type, a value, and a file. But we said Node strips the types without reading them. So where do they actually go?

This is a detour, to see what happens to a type once it is written.

On the left is the picture of one file and two jobs. The same main dot ts feeds two very different programs. One is tsc, the TypeScript compiler, whose job is to check: it reads every type and either reports errors or stays silent. The other job is erasing. Node does it every time we run the file, and tsc can do it too, writing the JavaScript out as a file. Either way the result is plain JavaScript, and V8 runs that, knowing nothing about types at all.

To see the erasing on screen, we ask tsc to write its output into a folder called emit. The terminal shows the command, and tsc prints nothing, which for tsc means success.

Now compare the two files. On top is the source, with the type of a box and the annotated values highlighted. Underneath is what tsc wrote. The Box type is simply gone, the colon and its type after the box have vanished, and so has the number after the padding. Every line that remains is the same JavaScript as before, with a semicolon added at each end. No checks are left behind, and nothing in the running program remembers that a box was supposed to have a numeric width.

That is the deal TypeScript makes. Types cost nothing at run time, because they are not there at run time. So the only time anything checks them is before the program runs. Next, we install the checker.

Node runs our file, but nothing has checked it yet. That is tsc's job, so we install it.

In the terminal, npm installs two packages as development dependencies: TypeScript, pinned to seven point oh point two, and the type definitions for Node itself, which tell the checker what Node's file system module looks like. npm reports four packages added in a fraction of a second, and the explorer gains a lock file and the node modules folder, greyed out because we never edit it.

tsc needs to know how to check, and that is the tsconfig dot json in the editor. It targets the newest JavaScript, uses Node's own module rules, and loads Node's types. Two options are highlighted. Strict switches on the full set of checks, the ones every serious TypeScript project uses. And no emit says: check only. Node already runs the file, so tsc should never write JavaScript next to it.

The side pane follows one run. tsc reads the config, then checks main dot ts and every file it imports, and ends in one of two places: a list of errors and an exit code of one, or silence and an exit code of zero.

We ask for the version, seven point oh point two, and then run the check. The last line of the terminal is the answer: nothing at all. Silence is tsc's way of saying the program is sound.

So now we have two tools reading one file. Next, we make them disagree.

Here is one small mistake, the kind a real program makes every day. In the highlighted line, the box's width is written in quotes, so it is a string rather than a number.

First, the checker. tsc stops at line five, column thirty-nine, exactly where the width is, with error TS2322: type string is not assignable to type number. The Box type said width is a number, and tsc held the value to it.

Now the same file, run with node. It does not complain at all. It strips the types, as we saw, and runs what is left. And the result is wrong in a way that is very JavaScript. The second highlighted line adds the padding to the width. With a number, eighty plus twenty-four is a hundred and four. With a string, the plus sign joins text instead, so the width becomes eight thousand and twenty-four. Node writes a box more than eight thousand pixels wide, and prints that size as if nothing had happened.

The side pane draws the two paths out of one file. The checked path refuses it. The run path draws it anyway. Underneath is the table to remember. A wrong type is refused by tsc and run by Node. A syntax error, a missing brace, is refused by both.

That is why the check is a separate step, and why it has to run before the program does. Node will not save us from a wrong type. But there is one kind of TypeScript that Node does refuse, and it is the next section.

Our box is about to get a colour, and many TypeScript tutorials would reach for an enum to name the colours. The editor shows one: an enum called Tone, with two members, source and store, and the box now carries a tone.

We run the file with node, and this time Node refuses. We asked it to leave out its own internal stack frames so the whole error fits, and what is left is the part that matters. It points at line three, underlines the enum, and names the problem: error unsupported TypeScript syntax. A TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode.

The side pane explains strip-only mode. Node's whole job here is deleting: it removes types and writes nothing new. On the left is everything it can delete. A type alias, a colon and a type, a cast with as: remove the characters, and valid JavaScript remains.

On the right is syntax it refuses, because it means something at run time. An enum becomes a real object, with a property for each member, so somebody has to write new JavaScript for it. The same is true of a namespace, and of a constructor parameter that declares a private field, which turns into an assignment. tsc knows how to emit that JavaScript. Node, which only erases, refuses.

So we have a rule worth keeping: write only TypeScript that can be erased. But right now, only Node enforces it, and only when the file runs. Next, we teach the checker the same rule.

The rule is simple: only syntax Node can delete. The question is who enforces it, and when.

The editor shows the answer, one new option in tsconfig, highlighted: erasable syntax only, set to true. It tells the checker to treat anything Node would refuse as an error.

The terminal runs the check again, on the same file with the same enum. tsc now stops at line three, column six, the word Tone, with error TS1294: this syntax is not allowed when erasable syntax only is enabled.

The side pane shows why that matters. One rule, two enforcers. Node enforces it when the file runs, and only then. tsc now enforces it while we write, in the editor and in the check, long before anything runs. The note says it plainly: the checker now refuses, up front, what Node would refuse only later.

This flag also explains a choice we will keep for the rest of the film. You will not see an enum here, or a namespace, or a constructor that declares its own fields. When we need named colours, in the next course, we will build them from a union of plain string values, which is erasable and, as it turns out, more precise.

That closes the first file. We have a package, a main file that draws one box, a checker with strict settings, and a rule that keeps the two tools in agreement. Next, we describe a whole scene in types.

Our engine is going to draw diagrams, and a diagram starts with a box. So the first thing to describe is one box, as plain values.

The editor holds five of them: an id, a title, a width, a padding, and whether the box is visible. Notice that none of them has a type written next to it. TypeScript does not need one. When a value is right there, the checker infers its type from it, and the side pane shows what it decides.

The interesting part is the difference between const and let. A const can never change, so TypeScript keeps the exact value as the type. The id is not just any string: its type is the single word orders. The width is exactly ninety-six. Visible is exactly true. Padding is declared with let, because it changes on the next line, so TypeScript widens it to number: any number may follow.

Those are the three primitive types we will use everywhere: string, number and boolean. Every other type in this film is built out of them.

The terminal runs the two steps we will use from now on. First the check, which is silent, so everything holds. Then the run. The first line prints the five values, with the padding now sixteen. The second line asks JavaScript itself what kind each value is, and it answers string, number, number and boolean. That is the run-time view, which is much coarser than the checker's.

That exactness is about to pay off. Next, we give the box a colour, chosen from a fixed set.

Every box in our diagrams has a tone, a colour family that says what the box is: a source of data, a store, a service. There are exactly seven, and anything else is a mistake.

The highlighted type at the top says so. Tone is a union of seven string literals, joined by vertical bars, and the bar reads as or. The side pane draws what that means: a type is a set of values, and this set has exactly seven members. Neutral, source, ingest, store, serve, consume and infra. Nothing else belongs.

So when the item declares its tone as a Tone and sets it to store, the checker agrees. And when a scratch file, try dot ts, makes the typo we all make, stroe, the terminal shows the result: error TS2820, type stroe is not assignable to type Tone. And then the checker adds a suggestion of its own: did you mean store? It can, because it knows the whole set.

Compare that with the last highlighted line. A variable called kind is declared with let and the word item. Because it may change, TypeScript widens it to string, the set of every text there is, and so the next line can set it to anything at all without a complaint. A wide type checks almost nothing.

The run prints the item with its tone in brackets: store, orders, Orders DB.

Seven allowed words is the first real rule our engine has. Next, we gather an item's fields into one shape.

Loose variables do not make a diagram. We need one value per box, with all its fields together, and a type that says what those fields are.

That type now lives in its own file, model dot ts, in a new source folder. The editor shows it. Tone has moved here, and under it is an interface called Item. An interface names a shape: an id that is a string, a title that is a string, and two fields with a question mark, sub and tone. The question mark means optional, and the side pane's table marks the difference: id and title must be there, sub and tone may be left out.

You could write the same shape with the type keyword and an equals sign instead. For an object, the two are nearly interchangeable. We will use interface for object shapes and type for everything else, which is the common habit.

The main file imports that type and builds the orders item, and the checker holds it to the shape. It has an id, a title and a tone, so it fits. The scratch file tries an item with a misspelled field, titel, and the terminal shows what happens: error TS2561. An object literal may only specify known properties, and titel does not exist in Item. Did you mean title? Mistyped field names are among the commonest bugs in JavaScript, and here one is caught before anything runs.

The run prints the same line as before, now read from one object. Next, we look closely at that question mark.

An optional field is a promise that the value might not be there. TypeScript takes that promise seriously, and so must we.

The side pane shows what the question mark really means. The type of an item's sub is not string. It is string or undefined, and every use of it has two branches. The orders item has a sub, one row per order. The API item has none at all.

The scratch file ignores that and asks for the length of the API's sub directly. The terminal shows the checker's answer: error TS18048, api dot sub is possibly undefined. In plain JavaScript that line would crash at run time with a type error. Here it never gets the chance.

The editor shows the two operators that handle the missing case, highlighted. The double question mark supplies a default: if the tone is undefined, use neutral. Then a plain condition builds the sub text only when there is one. And the question mark followed by a dot, optional chaining, stops early: if the sub is undefined, the whole expression is undefined instead of an error.

The run walks both items. The orders item has no tone, so it prints neutral, with its sub and a length of seventeen. The API prints serve, no sub, and a length of undefined, without a crash.

One item is not a diagram, though. Next, we put items inside a group.

A diagram has structure: boxes sit inside groups, and the groups sit side by side or stacked. That structure is a tree, and the next shape in our model describes it.

The editor adds an interface called Group, highlighted at the bottom of the model file. A group has an id and a title, a direction that is a literal union of row or column, and children. The children field is typed as Item followed by square brackets, an array of items. Every element must be an Item, and the checker will hold each one to that shape.

The side pane draws the value from the main file. The data group lays out its children in a column, and the column holds two items: orders and email. One parent, an array of children. That is a tree, even if for now it is only one level deep.

The main file prints the group's title and direction, then loops over its children with for of, and prints each one indented beneath it, with neutral as the default tone. The run shows the result: Data, in a column, then store orders and consume email, one step in.

The scratch file is gone, because nothing here is meant to fail. But look at the limit we just built in. A group can hold items, and only items. In a real diagram a group holds other groups too: a data center holds racks, and racks hold servers. Next, we let a child be either kind, and that needs a union of shapes.

A child in our tree can now be an item or a group. TypeScript can describe that, and the trick is a single field.

The model file gives each shape a type field with a literal value. Every Item has type item, and every Group has type group. Then the highlighted line names the combination: a SceneNode is an Item or a Group. And a group's children are now SceneNodes, so groups can hold groups, as deep as we like.

That type field is called the discriminant, and the side pane shows why it matters. A SceneNode on its own could be either shape, so the checker lets us read only the fields both share. But the moment we test the tag, the union splits in two. If type is item, it is an Item, with a title, a sub and a tone. If type is group, it is a Group, with a direction and children.

With that, the whole checkout scene can be written as data. It is in its own file in a new scenes folder: a browser, an API, a services group holding payments, inventory and a queue, and a data group holding the orders database and email. The tsconfig gains one setting, allow importing TypeScript extensions, because the main file now imports a value from a dot ts file.

The main file tests each top-level node's tag, and the run prints them: the browser and the API as items, then services with three children and data with two.

The test on the tag is called narrowing, and it is the next section.

The printer now turns the whole checkout scene into an outline, and it does that with narrowing: following the type through each branch of the code.

The function in the editor takes a node and a depth. The highlighted switch looks at the node's type field, and the side pane follows what the checker knows at each point. Before the switch, the node is an Item or a Group. Inside the item case, it is an Item, so the code may read its sub and its tone. Inside the group case, it is a Group, so it may read its children, and the function calls itself for each child, one level deeper. That is recursion, and it is how a function walks a tree whose depth it does not know.

Narrowing is not limited to switch. Inside the item case, a check that the sub is not undefined narrows it from string or undefined to string. A test with typeof, or with the in operator, which asks whether an object has a field, narrows the same way. The checker reads ordinary JavaScript conditions and updates the type to match.

The run shows the scene as an outline. Checkout on top, then the browser and the API with their subs, then the services group, in a column, with payments, inventory and the queue indented under it, and the data group with the orders database and email.

The printer handles every kind of node there is. Next, we add a third kind, and see whether the checker notices.

Our scenes need one more kind of node: a note, a short line of text that explains the diagram. Adding it shows one of TypeScript's most useful habits.

The model gains a Note interface, with type note and some text, and the SceneNode union grows to three members. The checkout scene opens with a note. But the printer's switch still handles only items and groups.

The highlighted default branch is what catches that. It assigns the node to a variable whose type is never. Never is the empty set: a type with no values at all. The side pane's table follows what the node can still be as the switch goes down. Before notes, after the item case only Group was left, and after the group case nothing was: never. So the assignment was fine.

With notes added, there is a leftover. After both cases, the node can still be a Note, and a Note cannot be assigned to never. The terminal shows the checker pointing at exactly that line, with error TS2322: type Note is not assignable to type never.

This is the payoff of a discriminated union. Whenever the model gains a new kind of node, every switch that forgot it becomes a compile error, at the line that needs the new case. Nothing slips through to run time unhandled. In a codebase with many such switches, that is the difference between a quick change and a hunt.

One more case for the note, and the outline prints it. Next course, we work out where each box goes.

Before the engine can draw a box, it has to know how big the box is. That is a job for a function, and functions are where TypeScript's types do some of their best work.

The new file, measure dot ts, holds two. The first is measure. Its parameters say what it takes: an item, and a padding with a default of twelve, so a caller may leave it out. After the parentheses, the return type says what it gives back: a Size, an object with a width and a height. Inside, it takes the item's title and sub, finds the longest line, and multiplies its length by nine point six, the width of one character in our monospace measure. Twenty pixels per line gives the height, and the padding goes on every side.

The side pane writes the whole function as one type: it takes an Item and an optional number, and returns a Size. That type is a value's type like any other, and later we will pass functions around by it.

The second function is row. Its last parameter starts with three dots, which makes it a rest parameter: any number of sizes, collected into an array. It adds up the widths, keeps the tallest height, and adds a gap between each pair.

The run measures each top-level item. The browser is a hundred and forty-nine by sixty-four. The two items in a row, with a gap of twenty-four, come to three hundred and thirty-two. And the email box with no padding at all is forty-eight by twenty: just its text.

Items are easy. Next, a group, whose size depends on everything inside it.

A group's size is not written anywhere. It is the sizes of its children, arranged in a row or a column, plus the group's own padding and title. And a child might be a group too. The natural way to compute that is a function that calls itself.

The new layout file has one function for every kind of node, called size of. The switch from Course 3 is back: an item measures its title and sub, a note measures its text. The highlighted group case is the interesting one. It loops over the children and calls size of on each, then combines them: in a row, widths add up and the tallest height wins, and in a column it is the other way round. Then it adds the gaps between children, room for the title, and padding on each side.

The side pane shows what happens when it runs on the services group. The call for services makes three more calls, one per child, and each child is an item, which returns straight away. That is the base case, the case that stops the recursion. Only when all three have answered can the group add them up. The call tree has exactly the shape of the scene tree, which is why recursion fits trees so well.

The run prints every top-level node. The note is two hundred and sixty-four by forty-four. The services group, three items stacked with two gaps, a title and padding, is a hundred and seventy-three by two hundred and ninety-six.

We have sizes. Next, we give every box a position, and keep them all in a map.

A size says how big a box is. To draw it, we also need where it is: an x and a y. Together they make a Rect, and the layout will produce one for every node.

The layout file gains a function called place. It works top-down: it records a node's rect, and if the node is a group, it walks across or down its children, handing each one its position. The results go into a Map, from a node's id to its rect. The side pane draws it: a key on the left, a rect on the right, ten keys in all, one per node.

A map has one property that matters a great deal. Asking for a key that is not there does not crash. It returns undefined. So TypeScript types the result of get as Rect or undefined. The main file deals with that honestly. It asks for the orders rect, and an if narrows it to a Rect before using it. The run prints orders at eight hundred and fifty-three, forty-four.

The scratch file takes a shortcut. After get, it adds an exclamation mark, the non-null assertion, which tells the checker: trust me, this is never undefined. The checker trusts it. But there is no node called cart. The terminal shows the result: a type error at run time, cannot read properties of undefined, reading x.

The exclamation mark does not check anything. It only silences the checker, so the crash moves to run time. Use it only when you can prove the value is there.

Next, a cleaner way to combine children: a function that takes a function.

The group case of size of had a loop with two running totals and an if inside. It works, but it says how rather than what. Higher-order functions, functions that take other functions, let us say what.

The editor shows two small arrow functions, row and column. Each takes two sizes and returns one: row puts them side by side with a gap, column stacks them. The highlighted line is the whole group case now. Map turns every child into its size. Then reduce folds that list down to a single size, using row or column depending on the group's direction. And the function we hand to reduce is just a value, chosen by a condition one line earlier.

The side pane follows the fold for the services group. Its three children are a hundred and forty-nine by sixty-four, the same again, and a hundred and forty by sixty-four. Reduce combines the first two with column, then combines the result with the third. What comes out is the widest width and the heights added with two gaps: a hundred and forty-nine by two hundred and forty. The padding and title then go around it, exactly as before.

TypeScript checks the plumbing. Reduce expects a function that takes two sizes and returns a size, and both row and column have that type, so either may be passed.

The run prints the whole layout with console dot table: every node, with its x, y, width and height. Services sits at six hundred and forty-four, and its children start twelve pixels in.

Next, a function that works for any type at all.

We keep needing the same walk: visit every node in the tree, ask each one a question, and collect the answers. The question changes, but the walk does not. A generic function lets us write the walk once.

The new file, tree dot ts, has a function called map tree. The angle brackets after its name introduce a type parameter, T. It stands for whatever type the question returns. The parameter f is a function from a node to a T, and map tree returns an array of T. Inside, it asks the node, then recurses into any children with flat map, so the answers come back as one flat list.

The side pane shows the payoff. In the main file, the first call asks each node for its id. The id is a string, so for that call TypeScript fills in T as string, and the result is an array of strings. The second call asks for each node's width, so T becomes number, and the result is an array of numbers. Nobody wrote string or number at the call. The checker inferred T from the function passed in.

That matters on the next line. Math dot max needs numbers, and because the widths are typed as an array of numbers, it is allowed. If the walk had returned something loose, that line could not be checked.

The run prints the ten ids, the ten widths, and the widest, two hundred and sixty-four, which is the note.

A type parameter can be anything. Sometimes we need it to be anything with a particular shape. That is next.

A scene's ids must be unique, or the layout's map would quietly overwrite one rect with another. A function that indexes things by id can check that, and it should work for nodes, rects, or anything else, as long as it has an id.

That is what the highlighted line says. Index by id takes a type parameter N, but the word extends puts a bound on it: N must have an id that is a string. Inside the function, that bound is what allows reading node dot id at all. Without it, N could be a number, and the checker would refuse.

The side pane's table lists what may be passed. An array of scene nodes is fine, because every node has an id. So is a list of plain objects with an id and a width, which have nothing to do with our model. The scratch file passes objects with a name instead, and the terminal shows the checker's refusal: error TS2353, name does not exist in a type with only an id.

The constraint has a second effect, just as useful. N is still the full type of what was passed in. So when the map of sizes is read back, the entry for queue is known to have a width, a number, not just an id. The run prints a hundred and twenty for it, and ten nodes indexed from the scene, with the browser's type read straight back as item.

A bound like that is how library code stays general without giving up its types.

Next, a walk that stops halfway through.

Map tree visits every node, whether we need them all or not. Sometimes we want to stop early: find the first title too wide for its column and report it. A generator walks the tree one node at a time, and only as far as asked.

The function in the editor has an asterisk after the word function. That makes it a generator. Instead of returning a list, it yields one node and pauses. Yield star hands over to a nested walk, so the children come out in order. Its return type says what comes out: a Generator of scene nodes.

The main file loops over it with for of. Each turn of the loop asks the generator for the next node, and the generator resumes exactly where it paused. The loop checks each item's title against a limit of eight characters, and breaks at the first one longer.

The side pane counts what happened. The loop visited the note, the browser, the API, the services group, payments, and then inventory, whose title is nine characters, and the run prints too wide: Inventory. Six visited. The four greyed-out nodes at the bottom, the queue, the data group, orders and email, were never reached. Breaking out of the loop stopped the generator, so no work was done for them.

That laziness is the point. A generator does no work until it is asked, and stops when nobody asks. On a scene of ten nodes it hardly matters. On a diagram of thousands, it is the difference between scanning all of them and scanning six.

Next, protecting a rect from being changed by accident.

Once the layout has placed a box, nothing else should move it by accident. In JavaScript, objects are shared, which makes that kind of accident easy. TypeScript can rule it out.

The side pane shows the trap. The scratch file loops over the map's rects, and the loop variable r is a second name for an object the map already holds. Two names, one object. So when the loop shifts every r forty pixels to the right, it is changing the layout's own rects in place, for everyone who reads them later. Nothing about that line looks dangerous.

The editor shows the defence, highlighted: the fields of Rect, and of Size, are now marked readonly. The objects are the same at run time, but the checker refuses any assignment to them. The terminal shows it catching the scratch file: error TS2540, cannot assign to x, because it is a read-only property.

So how does anything change a picture's position? By making a new value. The new fit file does that. Fit takes the content's size and a frame's size, keeps a margin of four percent on each side, and works out one scale and an offset that centres the content. The scale is clamped between a twentieth and four. It returns a fresh Transform and never touches a rect.

The run measures the content, a thousand and fifty-three by two hundred and ninety-six, and fits it into a frame of twelve eighty by seven twenty. The scale comes out at about one point one two, with the picture centred.

Next, a detour, to watch the whole layout happen.

This is a detour, to watch a whole layout happen, pass by pass, on a scene with a problem in it.

The scene is self, miniflow's picture of itself: a model, an engine group holding layout and route, and a draw step. One title, highlighted in the scene file, is a deliberate fault. It is sixty characters long, far wider than its neighbours.

The left side names the three passes. Measure goes bottom-up, because a parent cannot know its size until its children do. Place goes top-down, because a child cannot know its position until its parent has one. Fit comes last, and works on the finished picture.

For this lab, the layout logs every step, and the terminal shows the real order. Measure runs first: model, then the long layout item, then route, and only then engine, after both its children. The layout item measures six hundred by forty-four, so the engine group, which must hold it, grows to six hundred and twenty-four wide. Then place runs from the top: model at zero, engine next to it, its two children inside, and draw pushed all the way over to eight hundred and twenty-one, because the column in front of it grew.

That is the rule on the left: a title wider than its column grows the column, and everything after it moves over. Nothing is ever clipped, because clipping would hide words the author wrote. A diagram that grows too wide is fixed by the author, never silently by the engine.

Finally, fit scales the whole nine hundred and fifty-one by one eighty-eight picture into the frame at about one point two four. Next course, we draw it.

We have a rect for every box. To draw them, we need an SVG file, and building one well is a job with state: a size, and a growing list of elements. That combination, data plus the operations on it, is what a class is for.

The new file defines a class called SvgDocument. It has a width and a height, both readonly, and a list of elements, whose name starts with a hash, which we will come back to. The constructor runs when someone writes new SvgDocument: it stores the two sizes. Notice it assigns them one by one. TypeScript has a shortcut that declares fields in the constructor's parameters, but it is not erasable syntax, so with the rule from the first course, we write it out.

The methods do the work. Rect adds a rectangle element and text adds a text element, each built from a template string. Each ends by returning this, the document itself, so calls can be chained, as the main file does: rect, then text, on one line. A getter called size reports how many elements there are. Static empty belongs to the class rather than to any one document: it is called on the class name, and builds a document with no size at all.

The side pane draws the object after those two calls. Its element list has two entries, a rect and a text. To string assembles them into SVG, and the terminal shows it: the svg tag, the rect, and the text checkout. Then two elements, and zero for the empty one.

Next, that hash in front of elements.

The document's element list is its own business. Code outside the class should go through rect and text, never push strings into the list directly. TypeScript has two ways to say so, and they are not the same.

The first is the keyword private, which comes from TypeScript. The scratch file try private dot ts declares a small class with a private field, then reads it from outside. The second is the hash in front of a name, as in our document's elements. That one comes from JavaScript itself. The other scratch file tries to read the document's hash elements from outside.

The terminal shows what each costs. tsc refuses both, with two different errors: TS2341 for the private field, and TS18013 for the hash field, which says it has a private identifier.

But then we run them. Node strips types, and private is a type annotation like any other, so it is simply deleted. The first file runs and prints the supposedly private list. The second file never runs at all. Node itself rejects it with a syntax error: a private field must be declared in an enclosing class. The privacy is part of the language, so it holds even when no type checker ever looks.

The side pane sums it up. Private is enforced at compile time only. Hash is enforced at run time too. Our document uses the hash, because its list must stay consistent with what the methods wrote, whoever calls it.

The scratch files go. Next, one more trap waiting inside a class: the word this.

Inside a method, the word this means the object the method was called on. That sounds fixed. It is not, and our document is about to show why.

The editor adds two small methods. Box draws one rect, by calling this dot rect. Rects takes a list of rects and hands the box method to for each, to call once per rect. It reads naturally, and the checker is satisfied: the terminal's first line, the check, is silent.

Then we run it, and it crashes. The error points at line thirty-six, the inside of box, and says: cannot read properties of undefined, reading rect. This was undefined.

The side pane shows why. When we write doc dot box, with the object in front of the dot, JavaScript sets this to doc for that call. That is the left-hand case. But for each did not call doc dot box. It was handed the function alone, detached from its object, and it called it with nothing in front of the dot. So this was undefined. The value of this is decided by how a function is called, not by where it was written.

The fix is the line beneath: pass an arrow function that calls this dot box. An arrow function has no this of its own. It uses the this of the method around it, which really is the document. Every class-based codebase meets this bug, usually through an event handler or a callback, and the arrow is the usual fix.

Next, two renderers that share some code, through inheritance.

Our engine will have more than one way to draw a scene: the outline printer from the model course, and the SVG renderer we are building. They share some behaviour, and a class hierarchy is one classic way to share it.

The editor shows the base of that hierarchy. BaseRenderer is marked abstract, which means it cannot be created on its own: it exists only to be extended. It declares a name and a draw method, both abstract, meaning every subclass must provide them. It also has a protected method called label, which joins a title and a sub. Protected means subclasses can call it, but outside code cannot. And describe is a normal method, which every subclass inherits as it is.

The side pane draws the chain. The outline renderer extends the base, and its draw method is the printer from Course 3, now returning text instead of printing it. The SVG renderer extends it too, and draws every rect as an SVG rectangle, using the document class. Both are created in the main file with new.

The terminal shows inheritance doing its job. Describe was written once, in the base class, yet both renderers answer: outline, Checkout, five nodes, and svg, Checkout, five nodes. Then the outline renderer draws the full outline we know, and the SVG renderer produces thirteen lines of SVG.

It works. But notice the cost. Both renderers are now tied to the base class: change it, and both change. That is a strong coupling for one shared helper. Next, a looser way to say what a renderer is.

What do the two renderers really have in common? Not their code. They have a promise: each has a name, and a draw method that takes a scene and its rects and returns a string. An interface states that promise and nothing else.

The new file renderer dot ts holds it, highlighted. Interface Renderer: a readonly name, and draw, with exactly that signature. There is no code in it at all. The label helper, which the base class used to share, is now a plain exported function beside it. A helper does not need a class to live in.

So the base class is deleted, and the explorer no longer shows it. Each renderer now says implements Renderer instead of extends. Implements is a check, not a link: it asks the compiler to confirm that the class keeps the promise, and to complain at the class if it does not. Nothing is inherited, and nothing is shared at run time.

The side pane draws the new shape. One contract on top, two independent implementations under it. The main file holds them in an array typed as Renderer, and loops over it, calling draw without knowing or caring which one it has. The run shows both: three hundred and twenty-two characters of outline, starting with the scene's title, and nine hundred and ninety-one characters of SVG.

This is composition over inheritance. Small pieces that agree on an interface, rather than a family tree that must be kept in order.

And TypeScript lets us go further than most languages. Next, a renderer that never mentions the interface at all.

Here is something that surprises people who come to TypeScript from Java or C sharp. To be a Renderer, a value does not have to say so.

The main file adds two new renderers, both highlighted. The first is a class called Stats. It has a name and a draw method that reports how many boxes there are. It does not say implements Renderer anywhere. The second is not a class at all. It is a plain object literal called counter, with a name and an arrow function for draw.

Both go into the array typed as Renderer, and the checker accepts them. The terminal's first line is silent. The side pane's table explains why. TypeScript's type system is structural: a value fits a type when it has the right shape, whatever it is called and however it was made. Stats has a string name and a draw function that returns a string, so it is a Renderer. So is the object literal. The implements keyword on the other classes is only an early check, not what makes them fit.

Java and C sharp are nominal. There, a class is a Renderer only if it declares that it implements Renderer, by name. Two identical shapes with different names are different types.

The run shows all four renderers answering in the same loop. The outline, the SVG, stats with ten boxes, and counter with five top-level nodes.

Structural typing is why TypeScript fits JavaScript so well. JavaScript code passes plain objects everywhere, and TypeScript checks their shapes without asking anyone to rename anything.

Next, the SVG renderer draws the whole scene, properly.

Until now our SVG renderer drew bare rectangles. This is the section where miniflow draws its first real diagram.

The editor shows the new draw method. It works out the picture's size from the rects, plus a margin of sixteen on every side, and paints a dark canvas first. Then an inner function, visit, walks the scene. For every node, it fetches the node's rect, shifts it by the margin, and switches on the kind of node. A group gets a frame and a bold title, and then visit is called for each of its children. An item gets a rounded rectangle, its title in bright text and its sub beneath it in a muted colour. A note gets a dashed frame. Every element is a template literal, with the values dropped into the markup by dollar-sign braces.

The side pane follows the data: the map of rects from the layout, into visit, out as an SVG file. The main file writes it to out slash checkout dot svg, and the run reports two thousand and eighty-nine characters.

The bottom panel shows the result, opened in a browser. Everything the layout computed in Course 4 is now visible. The dashed note on the left. The browser and the API. The services group, with payments, inventory and the queue stacked in a column. The data group, with the orders database and email. Every box is exactly where the rect table said it would be, and every title fits its box, because the measure and the font agree.

But the renderer trusts its text completely. Next, a title that breaks the file.

The shop's checkout gets one more box, a cart, and its author writes the title the way a developer would: cart, inside angle brackets. It is a perfectly reasonable title. It is also a problem.

The highlighted line in the scene file is the whole change. The run still succeeds: main writes the SVG, a couple of hundred characters longer than before. Nothing in TypeScript complains, because to TypeScript the title is just a string, and any string is allowed.

But an SVG file is XML, and in XML a less-than sign starts a tag. The terminal runs xmllint, a standard XML checker, on the file, and it refuses. At line nine, opening and ending tag mismatch: Cart, and text. It shows the line, with the title pasted straight in between the text tags. Then two more errors follow from the first, all the way to premature end of data. A browser opening this file would show an error page instead of a diagram.

The side pane shows the gap between the two readings. The author meant six characters of text to display. The parser read an element called Cart that opens and never closes. The renderer pasted text into markup without saying which was which.

The fix is one function at the boundary, where text enters markup. It replaces the four characters that mean something in XML, the ampersand, less-than, greater-than and the double quote, with their escaped forms. Every string the renderer writes goes through it.

Next, that fix, and colour.

Every box has had a tone since the model course. Now the tones become colours, and the cart's title becomes safe text.

The new palette file maps each theme to its colours: a canvas, a group frame, ink, muted text, and then the seven tones, each with a fill and a stroke. The type it must match says every theme is a record of Tone to colour. That type is Record: an object with exactly these keys, all of one value type.

The highlighted last line uses satisfies instead of a type annotation. The difference is subtle and useful. Satisfies checks that the palette fits the type, so a missing tone is still an error. But it does not replace the palette's own inferred type with the wider one, so every exact key stays known to the checker.

The side pane quotes the check at work. A scratch palette with only six tones, missing infra, is refused with error TS2741: property infra is missing. Add a tone to the union, and every palette that forgets it fails, the same safety the never check gave our switch.

The renderer now looks up each item's tone in the palette, and passes every title, sub and note through escape XML on its way into the file. The side pane's table lists the dark theme's strokes.

The bottom panel shows the coloured checkout. The browser and the cart in the consume red, the API in amber, payments in violet, inventory in blue, the queue in cyan, and the orders database in green. The cart's title is drawn as text, angle brackets and all. And xmllint is silent now.

Next course, the arrows between the boxes.

A diagram without arrows is a list of boxes. This course connects them, and an arrow starts with a point.

A point is two numbers, an x and a y. We could use an object with two fields, but a pair in an array is lighter, and TypeScript has a type for exactly that: a tuple. The highlighted line in the new route file defines Pt as a readonly tuple of two numbers, and even names its two positions, x and y, so an editor can label them. An arrow that bends is then a list of points, a polyline.

The main file builds one, the bend in the side pane's table: four points, going right, then down, then right again. Destructuring pulls the first point out, and then its x and y, and the run prints them: x six hundred and twenty, y thirty-two. Two helpers in the route file do the work. Polyline turns the points into the text SVG expects, and length adds up every step. Because each step goes straight across or straight down, the length is just the sum of the distances, a hundred and twenty-eight.

The scratch file shows what the tuple type guarantees. A point with three numbers is refused with error TS2322: the source has three elements, but the target allows only two. And because the tuple is readonly, assigning to its first position is refused too, with TS2540. A point, once made, stays as it is, which matters when one point is shared by two segments.

Next, giving a rect a name, by joining two types.

The router will work with boxes by name. The layout's map knows each rect's id only as its key, and passing the two around separately is clumsy. What we want is a single value that is a rect and also has an id.

The highlighted line makes that type out of two existing ones. Placed is Rect, ampersand, an object with an id. The ampersand forms an intersection type: a value of it must have all the fields of the left side and all the fields of the right. The side pane draws it: x, y, width and height from Rect, plus the id, together in one shape.

An intersection is the counterpart of the union from the model course. A union says a value is one shape or another, so it may use only what they share. An intersection says it is both, so it may use everything. And just like the union, it does not exist at run time. The placed function simply spreads each rect into a new object with its id, and the type describes the result.

A second helper, centre, takes a placed rect and returns its centre as a point tuple, half the width across and half the height down.

The run prints two placed rects from the checkout. The API is at four hundred and fifty-two, zero, with its centre at five hundred and thirty-one and a half, thirty-two. The orders database is further right and down.

We have points and named rects. Before writing the router, a detour to see how one edge finds its way.

This is a detour, to follow one arrow from start to finish: from the queue to the orders database. The lab logs every step of the router, and the left side names them.

Step one: the two rects, fetched from the layout by id. The log shows the queue low down in the services column, and the orders database higher up, in the data column to its right.

Step two: the gaps between them, across and down. The log gives sixty-five across, and a hundred and twelve down. The first version of this router chose whichever gap was larger, and it went wrong: it sent this arrow out of the top of the queue and straight through the boxes above. So the rule is simpler. Boxes side by side are joined across, and only stacked boxes are joined up or down.

Step three follows from that: the faces. The arrow leaves the queue's right face and enters the orders database's left face, as the log says.

Step four, the ports: where along each face the arrow touches. The queue's right face has two arrows leaving it, so this one takes the first third. The orders database's left face has three arriving, so this one, coming from the lowest box, takes the three-quarter mark.

Step five, the path. Out of the queue to the middle of the gap between the columns, up to the height of the port, and across into the orders database. Four points, every turn a right angle.

The next three sections build each of those steps as code.

Now the router itself, and the first picture with arrows in it.

The scene model gains edges. An Edge has a from, a to and an optional label, and a Scene now has a list of them. The checkout lists nine: the browser to the cart, the cart to the API, the API out to the three services, the three services into the orders database, and the queue to email. The browser and the cart now sit together in a client group, so the picture stays narrow enough to read.

The highlighted function in the editor is the router. Route takes two rects and returns a list of points, and that is all. It picks the faces, takes an anchor point on each, and puts the bend in the middle of the gap between them. It reads nothing else and changes nothing. A function like that is called pure: the same rects in give the same points out, every time. The side pane draws it as rects in, points out, no state, and the note says why it matters. A pure function can be tested with nothing but two rects and an expected answer, which Course 9 will do.

The layout learns one thing too. Siblings with an edge running between them get a gap of thirty-two instead of twenty-four, to leave the arrow room.

The bottom panel shows the result. Arrows run from the client to the API, fan out to the services, and converge on the data. But look closely at the orders database. All three arrows arriving there aim at the same point, the middle of its left face, and their heads pile into one. Next, we spread them out.

Three arrows into one point read as one arrow. Each needs its own place along the face, called a port.

The new function in the editor is ports. It goes through every edge and works out which face it leaves and which face it enters, using the same faces function as the router. It groups the ends by face: all the ends on the orders database's left face land in one list. Then, highlighted, it sorts each list by where the other end sits, and spreads the ends out evenly.

The side pane's table works through that face. Three edges arrive, from payments, inventory and the queue. Sorted by the height of their sources, payments comes first, then inventory, then the queue. With three ports on one face, they go at one quarter, two quarters and three quarters of the way down. Sorting matters: if the ports were handed out in any other order, the arrows would cross each other on their way in.

The same thing happens wherever ends share a face. The API's right face has three arrows leaving it, and the queue's right face has two.

The router itself does not change. It already took a position along each face, defaulting to the middle, and now the renderer passes each edge its two ports.

The bottom panel shows the result. The three heads on the orders database are separate now, each where its line arrives, and the API's three arrows leave from three different points. The lines still share their channels between the columns. Giving each line its own lane is the next thing a serious engine does, and graphl-flow does exactly that.

Next, a nicer way to write an edge.

Most edges are just two ids. A few carry a label too. A small helper called edge makes both easy to write, and TypeScript can describe both ways of calling it.

The editor shows two signatures, highlighted, with no bodies. The first takes two strings, from and to. The second takes one object, with from, to and an optional label. These are overloads: the list of ways the function may be called. Below them comes the one real implementation, whose parameter types are wide enough to cover both. It checks which form it was given with typeof, and builds the edge either way.

Callers only ever see the overloads, never the implementation's own wider signature. That is the point. The checkout's edges are now written with the helper, and most read simply as edge, api, queue. The one from payments to the orders database uses the object form, to carry the label paid. The run prints three of the edges, and the labelled one shows its label.

The scratch file calls edge with a single id, which fits neither signature. The terminal shows the refusal, error TS2345. Notice the message talks about the object form, because when no overload matches, the checker reports against the last one it tried. Overload errors take a little practice to read.

Overloads are worth it when a function really has two distinct shapes of call, as this one does. When the shapes are close, a single signature with an optional parameter is simpler.

Next, an edge that points at nothing.

An edge names its ends by id, and ids are typed by people. The highlighted line in the checkout makes the typo that is waiting to happen: the API's edge goes to paymnet, with the n and the m swapped.

The checker has nothing to say. The first line of the terminal is silent, because every id is just a string, and paymnet is a perfectly good string. So the mistake reaches run time.

What happens there depends on us. Without a check, the renderer would look up the rect for paymnet, get undefined from the map, and crash somewhere deep in the router with a message about reading x of undefined, far from the cause. Instead, the renderer now checks every edge's two ends before drawing anything. When one is unknown, it throws a SceneError, a small class in the new errors file that extends the built-in Error, so it carries a stack and a message of its own.

The error also carries a cause. The second argument to its constructor is an options object, and cause holds the lower-level error, a RangeError naming the exact id that was not found. The terminal shows both. SceneError: edge two, from the API to paymnet, cannot be drawn. And underneath, in square brackets, the cause: no node has the id paymnet.

The side pane draws the path of the throw. Main called draw, draw threw, and since nothing caught it, the error unwound all the way out of main, and Node printed it and exited.

A typo in an id is the most common bug a diagram can have. Course 10 makes this exact one a compile error. Next course, scenes move out of code into files.

So far every scene has been TypeScript code. Real users of a diagram engine write data files instead, and reading a file means waiting for the disk. In JavaScript, waiting is done with promises.

The main file writes both scenes out as JSON, the checkout and a new one called self, miniflow's picture of its own pipeline. The highlighted function save is marked async, and its return type is a Promise of a number. A promise is a value that stands for a result that is not there yet. Inside, await writeFile pauses the function until the file is written, then carries on. Await only works inside an async function, or at the top level of a module like this one.

The side pane follows one read, step by step. Calling readFile returns at once, without the file: it hands back a Promise of a string. The terminal shows what that promise looks like when printed straight away: a Promise, pending. The file is not here yet. Then await pending pauses here, and while it waits, the rest of the program is free to run. When the disk answers, the function resumes with the value itself, a string, and the run reports reading back fifty-six lines.

The types follow the values exactly. Read file returns a Promise of string, and await turns that into a string. Forgetting the await leaves you holding the promise, a different type, and the checker will notice the first time you treat it as text.

The run also reports both files written: the checkout at two thousand three hundred and forty-one characters. Next, a detour: what is everything else doing while we wait?

This is a detour, to answer a question the last section raised. If await pauses a function, who runs in the meantime, and in what order? JavaScript has one thread, and a loop that decides what it does next. The lab makes that order visible.

The lab's script schedules four things, in this order: a timer for zero milliseconds, a file read, a promise that is already resolved, and a queue microtask call. It prints a line when it starts and another when it ends. Each scheduled thing prints a line when it finally runs.

The terminal shows the real order, and it is not the order of the code. Both sync lines come first, start and end, even though everything else was scheduled in between. That is the first rule, on the left: the call stack runs the script to its end, without a break. Nothing else can run until it finishes.

Next come the two microtasks: the resolved promise, then queue microtask. Promise callbacks run as soon as the stack is empty, before anything else gets a turn. Then the timer fires, even though zero milliseconds had long passed, because timers wait for the next turn of the loop. And last of all, the file arrives, when the disk answered, which is later still.

That is why await does not block. Pausing one function just returns control to the loop, and the loop goes on with the others. Every promise we await is a turn of this loop.

Back to the engine, and to the files we just wrote.

The scenes live in JSON files now, and the TypeScript scene files are gone. The new load file has one function: read the file as text, and hand it to JSON dot parse. The main file loads both scenes and draws each one.

People will edit those files by hand, and the editor shows the first thing people do. After the last edge, there is a comma, highlighted, with nothing after it. In TypeScript, that is perfectly fine. A trailing comma is allowed everywhere, and we have been writing them all film. But JSON is a stricter language than JavaScript, and it does not allow one.

The side pane draws what parsing is: text in, and either a value out, or a throw. The terminal shows both outcomes. Self is parsed and drawn first. Then the checkout fails, and JSON dot parse throws a SyntaxError. It shows line one hundred and twenty-eight of the text it was given, points at the closing bracket, and says the token is unexpected, quoting the end of the text, which is not valid JSON.

Notice what the checker had to say about this: nothing. A file's contents are only known at run time, so no compiler can check them. Every value that enters the program from outside, from a file, a network or a user, arrives unchecked. TypeScript's guarantees stop at that boundary unless we extend them ourselves.

The comma goes. But a file that parses is not yet a file that is right. Next, what parse actually returns.

The trailing comma is fixed. The next mistake is quieter: in the highlighted line, someone has set the API's title to forty-two, a number, without quotes.

JSON dot parse is happy with that. It is valid JSON. And the checker is happy too: the terminal's first line is silent. To see why, look at what JSON dot parse returns. Its return type is any. Any is TypeScript's escape hatch: a value of type any may be used as anything at all, and nothing about it is checked. Load scene returns whatever parse returns, so it returns any too, and the main file passes that any straight into the layout and the renderer.

The side pane follows the number on its way. From the file, through parse, through load scene, through the layout and the renderer, and not one check on the way. It finally meets code that relies on its type. Escape XML calls replace all on the title, and numbers have no replace all method. The terminal shows the crash: text dot replace all is not a function, inside escape XML.

That is the real cost of any. Not just that the bug got through, but where it surfaced. The error points at a function that did nothing wrong, three files away from the mistake, and says nothing about a title or about forty-two. On a big scene, finding the cause would take a while.

Any spreads silently through every value it touches. The fix is to never let it in. Next, the type that means the opposite.

The opposite of any is unknown. Both mean the value could be anything. But where any lets you do anything with it, unknown lets you do nothing, until you have checked.

The highlighted return type of load scene is now a Promise of unknown. The parsed value is the same at run time, but the checker will not let the main file pass it into the layout, or read a single field of it. So the load file gains type guards. A type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate, such as x is Scene. The highlighted guard checks that x is an object with a string title, an array of edges, and an array of nodes in which every node passes a guard of its own. If it returns true, the checker treats x as a Scene from then on. Above it, the node guard recurses into a group's children, and the item guard checks an item's id and title.

The side pane follows one value through. It starts as unknown, and nothing may be read from it. The guard is the evidence. When is scene returns true, the main file's if narrows it to a Scene, and it may be drawn. When it returns false, the file is skipped.

The terminal shows both. Self is drawn. The checkout, with its title of forty-two, is reported as not a scene, and skipped. Nothing crashes, and nothing three files away is blamed.

There is a weakness, though. Not a scene does not say why. On a file with a hundred nodes, that is little help. Before fixing that, one more way people get around unknown.

Checking every value with an if gets tedious, and people reach for a shortcut: as. The scratch file shows it. It loads the checkout and writes as Scene after the call. As is a type assertion. It tells the checker: this value is a Scene, take my word for it.

The checker does take its word. The terminal's first line is silent, and the scratch file runs: it reports the scene's five top-level nodes, and lays them out into twelve rects, title of forty-two and all. Nothing was checked. As is a claim, and here the claim was false, so the bad file walked straight through.

The editor shows the honest version of the same convenience: an assertion function. Its return type says asserts x is Scene. It runs the real guard, and if the value is not a scene, it throws. If it returns at all, the value is a Scene, and the checker knows it on every line below the call. The main file calls it once per file, with no if around it.

The side pane puts the two side by side. As Scene is a claim, checked by nobody. Asserts x is Scene is a proof, checked at run time, every time. The terminal shows the proof at work: self is drawn, and then the checkout throws a type error saying it is not a scene, and the program stops at the line that loaded it.

Use as only when you know more than the checker does, and can say why. For data from outside, use a guard or an assertion. Next, making the error say what is actually wrong.

A guard answers yes or no. A person fixing a file needs to know where it is wrong, and what was expected. That is a validator, and the key to a good one is a path.

The title of forty-two is fixed, but the checkout has three new faults, the kind real files collect. The editor shows the heart of the validator, highlighted. Check node takes a value, the path that leads to it, a list to collect errors in, and the set of ids seen so far. Every check that fails pushes a message that starts with the path. And for a group, it calls itself on each child, with the path extended by children and the child's index.

The side pane follows the walk into this file. The path starts at nodes. At nodes one, the client group, the direction is wrong: expected row or column, got rows. Inside the data group, nodes four, children one, the id is api, which the API itself already used, so it is reported as a duplicate. And because that box is no longer called email, the last edge, edges eight, points to no node called email.

The terminal shows the report, exactly as a person would want it. The file name, three problems, and each one with the path to the bad field. The validator does not stop at the first error. It collects them all, so a person can fix the file in one go instead of three runs.

Notice the validator is still plain TypeScript, built from the narrowing we already know. Every field starts as unknown and is checked before use.

One last step. Next, returning errors instead of throwing them.

Loading a scene can fail in three different ways: the file may be missing, it may not parse, or it may not validate. Throwing for all three forces every caller to remember a try. A Result makes failure part of the return type instead.

The errors file defines it, highlighted. A Result is a union of two shapes: ok true with a value, or ok false with errors. It is a discriminated union, the same idea as the scene nodes in Course 3, with ok as the tag. Two tiny helpers, ok and fail, build each side.

Load scene now returns a Promise of a Result of Scene or a list of strings. Inside, the read and the parse sit in a try.
